value.overview: The Slaty-tailed Trogon (Trogon massena) is a large, forest-dwelling trogon of tropical Central and northern South America. It is recognized by its green upperparts, red belly, and distinctive slate-gray undertail without the fine barring seen in several related trogons. In Costa Rica it is a resident species of humid lowland and foothill forests, where it often sits quietly on shaded branches and makes short flights to capture insects or gather fruit.
value.classification: The Slaty-tailed Trogon belongs to the family Trogonidae and order Trogoniformes. Several geographic subspecies are recognized, including Trogon massena hoffmanni, which occurs in Costa Rica and Panama.
value.identification: Adults have a broad red belly and vent, green back and head, and a long slate-gray tail underside. The male has a reddish bill, green head and upperparts, a red eye-ring, and a dark green or bluish breast band. The female is duller, with gray to dark slate upperparts and breast, a reddish lower belly, and a partly reddish bill. The unmarked slate-colored undertail is a particularly useful field character in Costa Rica.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southeastern Mexico through Central America to Colombia and northwestern Ecuador. In Costa Rica it occurs on both the Caribbean and Pacific slopes, especially in humid lowland and foothill forest, including mature evergreen forest, forest edges, and other well-wooded landscapes. It is generally found from sea level to about 1,200 meters, although local records may be concentrated at lower elevations. In the Área de Conservación Guanacaste, it has been observed around 300–700 meters in very humid forest.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and generally sedentary across its range. It may make local movements in response to food availability, breeding activity, or changes in weather, but it is not considered a regular long-distance migrant.
value.breeding: Breeding pairs excavate nest chambers in decaying wood, arboreal termite nests, or similar soft material, often several meters above the ground. Both adults may participate in preparing the cavity and incubating the eggs. Clutches usually contain two or three pale eggs. In Costa Rica, courtship and nesting are associated with the wetter part of the year, when insect prey, including caterpillars, becomes more abundant. Nesting dates can vary among regions and elevations.
value.dietFeeding: The Slaty-tailed Trogon feeds mainly on insects and other arthropods, including caterpillars, beetles, and termites. It also takes fruits and may occasionally consume small vertebrate prey. It commonly forages from low to high levels within forest vegetation, sitting motionless before making a short, direct sally to seize prey or picking fruit from a branch. Its broad bill and strong jaw muscles help it handle both animal and plant food.
value.behavior: This trogon often remains still for long periods on shaded perches, making it easier to hear than see. It usually forages alone, in pairs, or in small family groups. Courtship can include tail raising, feather fluffing, and mutual displays between the sexes. Its flight is typically short and direct between perches. The species uses a repetitive, low-pitched series of calls and may defend a breeding territory in suitable forest.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend has not been clearly quantified, but the species remains relatively widespread and is not currently considered globally threatened.
